procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 08.06.2016 of the High Court at Calcutta in CRR No. 64 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant challenged the Additional District & Sessions Judge, Fast Track Court, Calcutta's order before the High Court at Calcutta by filing a revision petition bearing C.R.R. No.64/2014 which was dismissed on 08.06.2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, convicted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, approached the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed his revision petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's judgment.

directions: Impugned judgment and final order of the High Court is set aside.
Bail bonds of the appellant stand discharged.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellant can be acquitted on technical grounds.

facts: The appellant was a vendor convicted for selling adulterated 'Pan Parag', a pre-packaged food item.
The appellant argued that he purchased the item in a sealed condition from the manufacturer, M/s Kothari Pouches Limited, and sold it as is.
He claimed protection under the law because the manufacturer had provided a written warranty for the product's quality, as evidenced by the purchase bill.
The prosecution argued that the appellant should not be acquitted on such 'technical grounds' and that a proper warranty in the prescribed form was not produced.
law: The Supreme Court relied on Section 19(2)(a)(ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

This section provides a specific legal defense for a vendor. It states that a vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offense if they can prove that they purchased the food article from a manufacturer, distributor, or dealer with a 'written warranty in prescribed form'.
application: The Court found that the appellant's situation fit the criteria for the defense provided in Section 19(2) of the Act.
It determined that the appellant, as a vendor, had successfully proven that the sealed 'Pan Parag' he sold was purchased from the manufacturer with a written warranty in the prescribed form.

The Court treated this statutory warranty not as a mere 'technicality' to be dismissed, but as a valid and substantive legal defense explicitly created by the Act to protect vendors who sell sealed goods in good faith.
By establishing that he had the required warranty, the appellant was entitled to the protection afforded by the law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument and acquitted him because he had a valid statutory defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The Court concluded that since the appellant had purchased the sealed product with a written warranty from the manufacturer, he could not be held liable for the adulteration, thereby overturning the convictions of the lower courts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the defense under the Act is unavailable to the appellant due to the non-production of a warranty from the manufacturer or distributor in the prescribed form.

facts: The appellant was a vendor who purchased a sealed, packaged food item, 'Pan Parag', from its manufacturer, M/s Kothari Pouches Limited.
The purchase was made through an invoice (Exhibit C/Annexure P-1) which contained a specific certification from the manufacturer.
The certification on the invoice stated: "We hereby certify that the goods mentioned in this invoice are warranted to be of nature and quality which theses purport to be."
The 'Pan Parag' sold by the appellant was later found to be adulterated, and the appellant was convicted by the lower courts.
law: Section 19(2)(a)(ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, provides a defense for a vendor.
This defense is available if the vendor can prove that they purchased the food article from a manufacturer, distributor, or dealer with a "written warranty in the prescribed form."
Section 14 of the Act requires manufacturers or distributors to provide such a warranty to the vendor.
application: The Court examined the argument that the appellant's defense was invalid because he did not produce a warranty in the prescribed form.
It reviewed the specific invoice (Exhibit C/Annexure P-1) used by the appellant to purchase the 'Pan Parag' from the manufacturer.
The Court found that the certification on the invoice, which warranted the nature and quality of the goods, was sufficient to meet the legal requirements.
The Court determined that this certification on the invoice constituted the "written warranty in prescribed form" as required by Section 19(2)(a)(ii) of the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the defense was unavailable. It held that the certification on the purchase invoice from the manufacturer served as a valid written warranty under the Act. Therefore, the appellant, having purchased the sealed item with this warranty, was entitled to the protection provided by Section 19(2) and could not be held liable for the adulteration.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the lower courts.

facts: The appellant was convicted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
The conviction was upheld in an appeal by the Additional District & Sessions Judge.
A subsequent revision petition filed by the appellant was also dismissed by the High Court.
This resulted in concurrent findings of fact against the appellant by three lower courts.
law: The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts unless a strong case for interference is established.
application: An argument was presented to the Supreme Court that there were concurrent findings of fact recorded by all the courts below.
Based on these consistent findings, it was argued that "No case for interference is made out."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument that it should not interfere. After hearing the parties and reviewing the record, it concluded that no case for interference was made out, thereby upholding the concurrent findings of the lower courts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be considered a 'vendor' for the purposes of the Act.

facts: The appellant purchased a food item, 'Pan Parag', from a manufacturer.
The appellant then sold this article of food to customers.
law: The Court acknowledged that the term 'vendor' is not defined in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
The Court referred to a previous Constitution Bench judgment (Mangaldas Raghavji Ruparel) which defined a 'vendor' as "the person who had sold the article of food which is alleged to be adulterated."
application: The Court applied the definition from the precedent case to the facts at hand.
It determined that since the appellant was the person who sold the article of food (Pan Parag) after purchasing it from the manufacturer, he squarely fit the definition of a 'vendor'.
The Court also noted that the appellant's own legal defense was based on Section 19(2) of the Act, which provides protections specifically available to a 'vendor'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the appellant was not a 'vendor' because his action of selling the food article directly matched the established legal definition of a vendor from a prior binding judgment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellant can be acquitted on technical grounds.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued for acquittal on grounds that the respondent characterized as 'technical'.
respondent_arguments: The appellant cannot be allowed to go scot-free only on technical grounds.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the defense under the Act is unavailable to the appellant due to the non-production of a warranty from the manufacturer or distributor in the prescribed form.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the defense under Sections 14 and 19 of the Act was available to them.
respondent_arguments: A warranty has to be given by the manufacturer or distributor in the prescribed form, and no such warranty was produced by the appellant, making the defense unavailable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the lower courts.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, by filing the appeal, argued that the Supreme Court should interfere with the findings of the lower courts.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere as there are concurrent findings of fact recorded by all the lower courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be considered a 'vendor' for the purposes of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that he was not a 'vendor', citing the Constitution Bench judgment in Mangaldas Raghavji Ruparel v. State of Maharashtra State, which defined a vendor as a person who has sold the article of food alleged to be adulterated.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued against the appellant's claim that he was not a vendor.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A certification on an invoice from a manufacturer, stating that the goods mentioned are warranted to be of the nature and quality they purport to be, constitutes a legally sufficient warranty to provide a vendor with the protection against prosecution available under Section 19(2)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central finding, which is presented as a conclusion without the preceding analysis in the provided text, is that the appellant had the protection available under Section 19(2)(a) of the Act. This statutory defense was sufficient to overturn the conviction, despite the food sample failing to conform to standards.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the test for the availability of a vendor's defense under Section 19(2) of the Act, which requires assessing whether the vendor purchased the article of food under a warranty.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that they were not a 'vendor' under the Act, siding with the respondent on this specific issue.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the appellant qualified as a 'vendor' for the purposes of the Act.
policy_considerations: The court implicitly rejected the policy argument that an appellant should not be allowed to go 'scot-free only on technical grounds', instead upholding the availability of a statutory defense as a valid basis for acquittal.
